title: Needle-felted harvest mouse
subtitle: A tiny round-bodied field mouse in ginger-brown merino, about 5 cm
excerpt: Needle felt a harvest mouse in warm ginger merino with a cream belly and large black bead eyes. At about 5 cm it is one of the smallest achievable needle-felted forms; the technique is beginner-friendly but rewards patience with the tiny face details.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from traditional needle-felting guild practice. Small rodent forms are a standard British needle-felting subject used in beginner workshops.

glossaryTerms.definition: A dry felting method using barbed needles to tangle wool fibres together without heat or water.
Wool drawn into a continuous ribbon; the standard input for needle-felting.

content.text: is a small round body in warm ginger-brown

with a cream underside, rounded ears, and large bead eyes. The finished mouse is about 5 cm from nose to rump, sitting upright. The small scale demands a fine needle (size 40) for detail work, but the form itself is forgiving to build.

attrs.title: Needle safety
attrs.body: Stab straight in and out at 90 degrees. Use the finger guard; at this scale fingers are very close to the needle tip.

items.name: Strong thread and needle for bead eyes

content.text: Take a small amount of ginger roving and roll it into a compact oval. Needle felt on all sides until the body is firm and about 3.5 cm long and 2 cm across at the widest point. The harvest mouse body is rounder and more egg-shaped than a house mouse; resist lengthening the body as you work.

Roll a small ball of ginger roving and needle it into a slightly domed round head, about 1.5 cm across when firm. Attach it to the front of the body by pressing the join firmly and needling through from all directions. The head should sit proud of the body, not sink into it. Build a very small rounded muzzle by applying a little extra roving and needling it into a gentle bump.

Needle two small flat discs of ginger roving on the mat, each about 1 cm across. Add a tiny amount of pink roving to the centre of each to suggest the inner ear and needle it in. Attach the ears to the top of the head by needling the base of each disc into the skull from both front and back. The ears should stand slightly away from the head rather than lying flat.
Step 4: Cream belly and face detail

Needle a thin layer of cream roving along the belly and up the front of the muzzle. Keep the edges clean. Needle a small cream or white area around the muzzle tip to define the face. Work slowly at this scale: too much cream obscures the face proportions.

Stitch the black bead eyes into position on either side of the head, just above the muzzle line, using strong thread pulled tight through the head. Needle a tiny indent at each nostril with the size-40 needle. Add a thin rolled tail of ginger roving, about 4 cm long, and needle it to the base of the body. Harvest mice have proportionally long tails relative to their body length; the tail adds a great deal to the recognisability of the finished piece.

items.problem: The body came out too elongated
items.cause: Needling from the sides while the form was soft, which stretched the roving lengthways before it compacted
items.fix: Start with the core rolled tightly, and needle from the ends inward to establish the round shape before needling the sides.

items.cause: The attachment point was needled from the front only, so the ear is loose at the back
items.fix: Needle the back of each ear base firmly into the skull to hold it upright from behind as well as in front.
